items.title: Austin trip day two: I ask to pay with bitcoin and someone tried to choke me
items.text:
Hey stackers,

Writing from the poker room after a four hour session. Taking a long break before I head back. Here’s my favorite hand from the sesh if you’re interested:

https://stacker.news/items/1603097/r/SatAttack?commentId=1603670

I woke up later than I wanted to knocking on my hotel door. It was 930 and housekeeping wanted to clean my room. I politely declined, got out of bed, brushed my teeth and quickly made my way out. There were things to see and bitcoin to spend. @plebpoet had recommended Caffe Medici as a place you can buy coffee and pastries for sats so that’s where I went first. There’s three locations and with some poking around I found the origional one. It’s in a nice quiet part of town and the ambience from outside looked really cool.

Here’s their BTCmap: [https://btcmap.org/merchant/way:382559089](https://btcmap.org/merchant/way:382559089)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163624)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163625)

I loved these stone chairs and tables. I wish I could have captured them all but some were being used and I didn’t want to take pictures of strangers. Inside was really nice too. Lots of plants and plenty of seating. I head to the counter where I see their square terminal and order a red eye which if you don’t know is an espresso shot with a regular coffee poured over it. It will clear the mind and wake up the bowels. Good for the morning. Right in the middle of asking if she would accept bitcoin she rings me up and answers my question; I see that wonderful toggle in the top left of some square terminals. I toggle to Bitcoin and I’m presented with a lightning address. I pay it with Phoenix no issues.

I asked her how often people pay with bitcoin—not very often, I guessed. She said only some times. She had been working there for four months and I was the third person to pay with sats. Not bad actually, I thought. It’s not like she rings everyone up, so there could have been others.

After a few sips of coffee and a couple pages from the second book of the Outlander series by Diana Gabaldon, I realized I had forgotten to check the parties! Fool boy. I asked where they came from, I don’t remember the name, but they get them from a local bakery here in Austin. I ended up with a blueberry muffin and toggled over to Bitcoin and sent another successful transaction.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163627)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163628)

I had plans to go to jiujitsu at the Austin 10th planet at 11 but waking up late was really deterring me from executing that plan. I really wanted to skip the workout and stay on this couch with my book and coffee. I read and read some more and checked the time. It was 1030. The gym was only 15 min away. There was time to not skip…. Over to my left I notice they have whole beans for sale on the shelf and decide there. I’ll
Buy some beans and stop being lazy. After the third lightning transaction in the last hour she tells me you get a free coffee with a bag of beans purchase….. UuuUgh it really sounded nice to sit and read with my free cup. Instead I take it to go and head to the gym.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163629)

I arrive at the gym 10 minutes before class time. I didnt bring a rash guard so I needed to buy one and told the guy over the counter as much. I asked if I could pay for both with bitcoin and he was a bit hesitant. “I think so” he said. He’s showing me the options for rash guards that are hanging on the racks when I see a box on the floor with some orange and black material inside. The box is labeled “b-coin”

Are these rash guards?! I ask
Oh yeah, they are. You want one of those?
Uuuuh YEAH. He pulls one out and shows it to me and it’s AWESOME. Here it is on me:

![](https://m.stacker.news/163630)

He had to text the owner and inquire about my bitcoin request. She responded pretty quickly and texted him a QR code made by cash app. The ones that you can pay either lightning or on-chain to. I took the opportunity to save some liquidity from my Phoenix channel and paid on-chain with Blue Wallet. I told him he should let her know I made an on-chain payment and that I was confident she’d be ok with that. And that she should receive the payment in about ten minutes. I paid 3sats/vB to ensure that was accurate.

Equipped with my new sweet rash guard it was time to start class. Everyone was very welcoming in introductions and we got to work pretty quickly. We warmed up with some bridges and shrimps and got right into the lesson. Today we were going to work on getting a hip toss from full guard and failing the attempt some attacks you can do instead.

My partner was great, I wish I remembered his name. I’m fairly novice, and he was patient and helped me with some important details on the attacks we were learning. We went over locking the Americana after the failed hip toss, then the guillotine, the triangle, the kimura, and omaplata all stemming from the original hip sweep attempt from full guard. during practice  I took a nasty elbow to the lip that swelled right away and filled my mouth with an iron taste (wear a mouthguard kids). Lesson complete, the next hour was open mat. They started the 5 min repeat clock and let people get sparring rounds in. I did a couple before hit hitting the showers. I’m a bit out of jiujitsu shape haha. Awesome stuff. Awesome class. Thanks coach Curtis!

![](https://m.stacker.news/163631)

On my way out the gym coach Curtis was at the front desk. I had asked him earlier for this group picture and told him I will
Blog about my day today on a forum. “Blog or vlog?” He asked.

Blog.

“People still read?” Haha YES I told him. And I told him where I’d blog as well I told him about stacker news and what it’s like. I told him the idea that because valuable things are used to express like-ness valuable content surfaces to the top. I showed him my stacker news and made a couple zaps. He was really intrigued. “A negligible amount I assume, like a small amount of sats?” Ummmm YES SIR. I was happy to hear him use the word sats. Bitcoin was normal for him, it seemed. He said he will check it out and that seemed like the perfect opportunity to give him one of the SN stickers @k00b gave me yesterday. He loved the sticker and joked about putting it up on the stall door so people were forced to see it. I’m sure he was joking but I really hope that happens. Then he asked me if I was the guy who paid with bitcoin today. I said yes and he goes “ok let me hook you up” (!!!)

He said anyone repping and using bitcoin he wants to help out. Wow… awesome. He starts digging around in the “b-coin” bin looking for a pair of shorts to give me. They didn’t have my size, unfortunately, and so he offered a long sleeve rash guard instead. I had to decline. I have many rash guards back at home and I didn’t want to take one just because it was free. He told me I can come back to the gym for free while I was on my trip… I was so grateful. How cool! He showed me around the gyms grocery store which was actually rather stocked. They had grass fed beef. They order by the cow and sell frozen beef from the gym. They had raw milks and other treats. Loaves of bread. All sorts of locally made goods. He told me the raw milks were made by a lady who loves bitcoin and sometimes they use Bitcoin to transact with her. Hooter Flats was the name of her company. I bought one of the chocolate milks. Perfect post-training snack.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163632)

Workout complete I wanted to head to play some poker but I needed to eat first. I pretty quickly decided to head back to the Green Mestique from yesterday and get the same thing but different meats. I ordered the turkey, chopped beef, and the sausage. I had to get that sausage again. For sides I got potato salad and repeated the green beans as well. When they brought my plate they had given me chicken  instead of the turkey. No matter, I knew it was great. I couldn’t resist putting the BBQ sauce all over the chicken even though it stung like hell the cut on my inner lip. But I worked through the tears and finished strong.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163634)

And that’s day two! I went to the poker room after this and I am just now starting another session. I’ll probably play a couple hours before heading to bed.

If you missed my day one report check it out here: https://stacker.news/items/1602995/r/SatAttack

See you stackers, thanks for reading.

items.title: [Read-along] The Odyssey, W.H.D. Rouse, Books IV - VI
items.text:
*If you've been following along--catch up on the last* [part](https://stacker.news/items/1595925/r/billytheked)*--you probably have found this to be a relaxed pace of reading. Maybe more so than you wish. Alas, life has way of keeping me from this project. As mentioned before, I am reading a hard copy of the translation of W.H.D. Rouse, but I can also recommend the* [*digitized version of the translation of A.S. Kline.*](https://www.poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Greek/Odhome.php)

***

In the next three books, finally we meet Odysseus, who is (reluctantly?) biding his time on some island with a nymph named Calypso. We hear from his peer, Menelaos and Helen, how Odysseus' heroism and restraint delivered them to victory against the Trojans; however, it becomes harder to distinguish who the true Odysseus really is. His tendency to appear differently from his true nature begins to reveal itself in the stories told about him, and now, first hand, as we are taken along on his adventure to meet the Phaiacians. Thus, we begin to find some truth in the first line of the poem, as translated W.H.D. Rouse, 'here is the story of a man who is never at a loss.' Odysseus begins to earn the name he bears (ὀδύσσομα), whose meaning in Greek translates into something like "to be hated."

## Discussion on Themes

**Hospitality**
The vivid descriptions of feasting, drinking, and making sacrifice to the gods upon the arrival of a guests has defined the escapades of Telemachos up to book IV in the poem. Even as he goes to the house of Menelaos, his good manners and refined appearance precede him, even before he has the chance to make himself known as the son of Odysseus. The Odyssey, being the "national" epic of the Achaeans, takes painstaking effort to provide encyclopedic, lurid descriptions of the level of civilization that had been achieved by Greeks at that time. Clearly, the poem paints a complete and detailed picture of their cultural achievement in the deeply entrenched and refined mores that consistently define what it meant to be Greek. This cultural consistency stands in contrast to the geographic and political separation of the different kingdoms that existed at the time.

**Appearances versus reality**
Finally, in Book V, the reader gets their introduction to Odysseus, who, despite his loyalty to his wife, is on some island playing house with the Nymph Calypso. Since Odysseus rarely presents himself as he truly is, it is impossible for the reader to differentiate whether his desire to return home is authentic, or some hollowed-out sense of moral duty. The reader first learns of his duplicity when Helen recounts how he sneaked into Troy disguised as a beggar, revealing to her their plans to sack the Trojans and rescue her. Also, when Calypso, tells Odysseus he can return home as long as he concedes that his wife is not prettier than her, he lays with her, and doesn't resist. Again, as Odysseus approaches Nausicaa in book VI, he appears as a homeless beggar, in want of proper clothes, when in fact, as we know, Odysseus is the center of attention on Mt Olympus.

**The sea/landscape both as friend and enemy**
There is this sense in the poem that the god of the sea, Earthshaker Poseidon, is the single chaotic force that the Achaeans owe their greatness to, as well as their woes. Nausicaa says to her maids that there is no mortal enemy who do harm on Phaiacia since their country is out of reach, "far away at sea." Also, despite Zeus and Athena's desire to see Odysseus return home, it is grumpy old Poseidon who hurls continued misfortune upon him, as seen after he leaves Calypso. The poem uses the "wine-darkened" sea as a representation of a kind of frontier of civilization, acting at the same time as a buffer of defense, but also a liminal and chaotic realm, where just about anything can happen.

## Questions for contemplation

* **How do you define the frontier of civilization now? Is it a physical place/thing, technological, or something else?**
* **What American national epics document the height of its culture and civilization? How would you characterize these works?**
* **In your opinion, how should we read Odysseus' trickery, as a mark of virtue or a vice?**

# Summaries

## Book IV

Menelaos recounts the death of his brother, Agememnon and laments Odysseus' apparent death, not knowing that he is talking to the latter's very own son. Helen of Troy sedates everyone present with some kind of drug she picked up in Egypt, and tells them the story Odysseus in Troy, where Helen, being held captive, recognized Odysseus disguised as a beggar, who was able to tell her of the Greek's plan to sack the city. Menelaos recounts how he heard her as she circled and touched the Trojan horse, calling our his name, and that if it weren't for Odysseus's being there, urging restraint, he would have called back, blowing their cover. He then tells the story of how he tricked the Old Man of the Sea in Egypt, disguising himself and two of his men with seal carcasses so they can ambush him while he is asleep. The Old Man tells Menelaos of Agememnon's murder, and how Odysseus was still living. Penelope, back in Ithica, prays to Athena, as her suitors plot against Telemachos, laying in wait for his ships to return. Athena summons the ghost of Iphthime, daughter of Icarus, to visit Athena in her sleep to inform her that she will protect Telemachos from harm.

## Book V

Zeus and Athena discuss Odysseus' fate. Zeus reluctantly agrees to intervene to by sending Hermes to inform Calypso of their desire to see Odysseus find his way home, on the condition that Odysseus travel without man or god, and only after a good dose of bad fortune. Calpyso tells Hermes that she loves Odysseus, but does not wish to anger Zeus. She tells Odysseus that it is the god's will that he be allowed to go home, but that he must admit she is prettier than his wife, which he does, and the sleeps with her. Calypso send him off, helping him to hew trees and craft a ship, supplies him with food and wine and water. Poseidon sees Odysseus thus returning, close to his destiny, and decides on shaking up his world, sending a storm his way, to throw him off course. Ino, or Leucothea, the White Sea Goddess, takes pity on him, orders him to strip his clothes and gives him a veil that helps him swim to safety. At first Odysseus refuses, choosing to test his fate and his trusted raft, but this quickly shatters like straw on the threshing floor, and he takes Ino's advice. After he swims to safety, he kisses the earth, returns the veil to Ino, prays to Zeus, and finds a place to take shelter, collapsing from exhaustion.

## Book VI

In the house of Alcinoos, king of the Phaiacians, sleeps his daughter, Nausicaa. Athena visits her in a dream to inspire her to take all of her best bridal linens down to the river to be washed, for the time is coming when she must be prepared to be wed. Thus, Nausicaa appeals to her father, who allows this, prepares for her carts and donkeys. She and her maids take the linens down to a rushing stream, bathe, lather in olive oil, and adorn themselves as the goddess Artemis, daughter of Zeus. They begin playing ball, when Athena decides that it is time that Odysseus is awaken. She causes one of them to drop the ball, sending it hurling down toward the eddies, awakening him. He emerges, craggy and briny, approaches the women, all who get scared away except for Nausicaa, whose fear Athena removed. Odysseus, impressed by her refinement, makes an appeal to her for clothes, which she agrees to. He washes and changes, and Athena makes him taller and more handsome. Finally, the latter invites Odysseus to return to Phaiacia among her party, instructing him to hide in her father's orchard until she makes it back to her father's house. She gives him instructions on how to find her, and tells him he must supplicate himself to her mother if he wishes to return to his own people.

items.title: Plenty of success with square bitcoin payments.
items.text:
Hey guys. Wanted share a nice place on Solomon’s island Maryland called Juice buzz if you’re ever in the area. Here’s their BTCmap: https://btcmap.org/merchant/node:13576086075

I spend bitcoin there often and I am still running into new staff members at the register there. They have the toggle option that makes everything so easy and smooth. I just had a nice interaction and wanted to share.

They make their own great juices so I got one of those and they do smoothies as well. I got a berry blast with creatine. When the lady rung me up she said scan or tap and I responded with the same thing I always do here:

Actually I’m gunna pay with bitcoin, isn’t that cool?

That is cool! She exclaimed, which made me smile.

So she presented the pay page, I toggled to Bitcoin, and having pre-opened my Phoenix wallet I scanned it right away. I like to hold the phone up so they can see me press pay and witness the speed.

She gasped and said Wow that was really fast!

Right?!

Then I like to give a cool spiel that always seems to be accepted well without me feeling or acting like a salesman.

I told her that jack Dorsey is the creator of cash app and also square and he is a nice advocate for bitcoin—new information for her.

I told her what’s cool here is that we are using an inclusive network. Before, in order to interact with a Cash App bar code, I would need cash app. Venmo to Venmo. Cash app to Cash App. Examples of exclusive networks. But what’s cool about Bitcoin is anyone can use it and in many different ways. You can use any one of the hundreds of apps out there like I did or if you have the skill and desire you can build your own and interact in the same way we just did.

She was interested! But she did say skeptically: yeah I’m not really too sure about bitcoin.

I said that’s understandable. It’s weird and intimidating and controversial and there’s lots to learn.

I continued to say one of my favorite things about Bitcoin though is that anyone can use it. Your age, sex, race, religion, location matters not. Bitcoin will work for anyone without permission or ID.

She asked: but do you need cash app to have Bitcoin?

No, Bitcoin is completely separate from everything else I said. And left it at that.

Juice buzz is owned by Dana the owner of the Blue Wind Gormet. I wrote about her and that place twice in the past. Here’s the links:

https://stacker.news/items/1436254/r/SatAttack

https://stacker.news/items/1472530

These places right now are my favorite places to spend sats. As far as I know Dana is still keeping the bitcoin she receives through her square terminals and isn’t converting. I have tried to encourage her to buy honey from [https://sweetsats.io](https://sweetsats.io), a bee farm in Maine, to use in both of her stores so she can have somewhere to spend her sats, but I don’t think it’s happened yet.

items.title: Austin trip day six: lakes, hikes, final bitcoin meal.
items.text:
Hey stackers,

I write from the airport terminal in route to the chilly easy coast. What an incredible trip this has been. I’m normally looking forward to getting back home and returning to the recurrence of every day life. Not this time. I am not ready to leave and I know I’ll be back. Perhaps to live one day.

Yesterday morning I woke up at 3 AM a little hung over from all my wine at III forks and I couldn’t sleep. So I went to play poker. Got there at 4 AM and the crowd was wild. Everyone had been there since the night before and everyone seemed drunk, tired, or both. I played this huge hand and ended up winning a $1400 pot. https://stacker.news/items/1606387/r/SatAttack?commentId=1606424

I played until about 7 AM and headed out for breakfast. I ended up at a really nice diner called Phoebes diner and had a great meal. Forgot take pictures though. They sell slab bacon and serve it in thick deep fried slices. Wonderful. I get back to the hotel and sleep from 830AM to 12PM. @grayruby had recommended I take the 30 minute drive to visit lake Travis. After poking around on my phone for things around there I found a hike and a restaurant I wanted to do.

Here’s the all trail for the hike: [river place nature trail](https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/texas/river-place-canyon-trail?sh=true)

The hike ended up being a great success. The weather was great and it was just the right amount of challenging to get the heart pumping.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164323)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164324)

I’ll take a little time to plug the Earth Runners here. For all my barefoot maxis out there this is a wonderful footwear for rocky environments where bare feet may have a tough time. I have taken these everywhere in all sorts of terrain. Love them.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164326)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164327)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164328)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164329)

Awesome hike. I was pleased to find good water flow and was surprised how clear it was! That tree going across the path is called the noggin knocker and there was a sign warning you not to knock your noggin haha.

Finishing my hike I was very ready for food and water and headed out to a restaurant right on Lake Travis called The Oasis. I didn’t really know what I was getting myself into but this place was GRAND. It’s a massive four story restaurant that’s the size of a big hotel. All four stories have a balcony that over looks the lake. There’s awesome art and decorations everywhere.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164331)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164332)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164333)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164334)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164335)

On my way in there was this blue metal UFO thing covered in stickers. I took the opportunity to put one of the stickers @k00b gave me on there. Turned out nice I think.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164336)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164337)

The food was decent. I got the chips and salsa. (Great chips!!) the chicken enchiladas with rice and beans, and a margarita on the rocks. I wasn’t planning on drinking but… the view made me.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164338)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164339)

I got back to my hotel around 6 pm and slept until 830. I had been deliberating between going to play poker one last time or going to find one last place to spend some sats. The issue was they were in opposite directions and I was really torn for a while. With one last check of BTCmaps I found a great solution. A place called Rockin Rolls that wasn’t in the downtown areas! It was close enough to the hotel and poker room to do both. So off I went. Here’s the BTCmap link [https://btcmap.org/merchant/node:13309320506](https://btcmap.org/merchant/node:13309320506)
It’s a small food truck in small gathering of food trucks right off the road. I appreciated the abundance of parking here!

![](https://m.stacker.news/164342)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164343)

These guys are awesome and if you’re a pizza eater in Austin I recommend giving this one a try. They make sourdough pizza rolls and they are very good. I ordered three classics (pepperoni and cheese) and a mini cannoli. Now time to pay. I see they only have the small white square terminal and I won’t be presented with the toggle option so I tell the man I’d like to pay with bitcoin if I can… he isn’t sure and calls the owner over who was thankfully there. He says “I think I set that up …” and we collectively poke around the terminal. Doesn’t take us long to find Bitcoin listed as one of the payment options and I tell them all we have to do is click that and it should generate me a QR code. It did and I made another seemless Phoenix payment. I gave my small spiel about how cool this is and how anyone who knows how can interact with this terminal with a bunch of different options.

The owner, Jake, was impressed and pleased. He was excited to see bitcoin being used and told me I was the first to do it. But on BTCmaps someone had verified the location in November 2025 so I was thinking perhaps not. I showed him BTCmaps and his little page on there and he thought that was very cool too! I told him that I would be blogging about this day and experience on stacker news and gave him the lowdown about what goes on here. “That sounds right my ally” he said. He loves community and according to him he likes crypto. He’s an ethereum guy he says. I told him I don’t know anything about it because I haven’t been able to move past Bitcoin. I was explaining what SN was and he understood immediately. “So instead of a like you just send over a little satoshi?” YEAH! I gave him a SN sticker and told him how to find us and that if he ever had any questions or inquires about using bitcoin in his business or other wise this is the place to come. I told him he would be very welcomed as a business owner accepting sats.

When I got my order I realized I didn’t have a drink. I asked for a bottle of water and had opened my Phoenix wallet to pay but he just said don’t worry about it. Thanks Jake!

I’ll say again, if you like pizza, come try this place. It’s awesome and he was telling me he’s looking to move to another state. Him and his wife love Austin but they’ve been there for 20 years and are ready for change. So time is running out!

![](https://m.stacker.news/164347)

After my pizza rolls it was time for one last poker sesh. I headed back to the lodge card club and played an uneventful 1.5 hours and won $10. I got gas for  the Turo rental, got to my hotel around 1130, and packed up. I had to be up at 530 to head to the airport.

I enjoyed my time in Austin very much and I really enjoyed sharing my experience here on stackers!! I’ve gotten a lot of support and a lot of engagement and that has been sweet. Thanks for reading and thank you to those who gave me awesome suggestions. I tried to do them all.

items.title: There is No Such Thing as Price Gouging: Airline Shutdown Edition
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/166604)

![](https://m.stacker.news/166605)

I saw a lot of economically ignorant tweets surrounding the recent shutdown of all flights nationwide by the FAA, so it's good time to re-iterate: there is no such thing as price gouging.

The rise in price of Ubers, hotel rooms, or supplies during any kind emergency is simply the product of demand rapidly rising, while supply remains fixed in the short term. Anyone who has seen a supply & demand graph can understand this phenomenon.

![](https://m.stacker.news/166611)

Moreover, it is good for victims of a disaster if you allow prices to rise.

Let's say a hurricane hits town, and the price of a gallon jug of water goes from $1 to $10. People from other towns will see an opportunity, and bring supplies from their town to sell for profit. But if you ban it under the guise of "price gouging," you're killing the incentive to do so, and, ironically, depriving the affected people of needed supplies. You're also creating a perverse incentive for whomever gets the store first to buy up a larger supply of water than they personally need, just because it's so cheap.

items.title: Exact-Channel Circular Rebalancing for Alby Hub
items.text:
Not sure who else might need this, but...

I built Grynvault Rebalance on top of Alby after the swap-backed rebalance option I used to use disappeared since boltz went down. I still had liquidity, but on the wrong sides of my channels—and ordinary routing could not guarantee which local channel sats would leave through or return through.

RC.7 is an experimental Alby Hub v1.24.3 fork for embedded-LDK operators. Choose the exact outgoing and returning channels, find a non-paying local route, review a fresh fingerprint-bound quote and projected balances, then approve one execution. It includes fail-closed migration and recovery hardening from upstream review.

It cannot create liquidity or guarantee a public route: you need one channel with outbound liquidity, another with inbound capacity, and a viable path.

macOS 15.4+ for this RC. PGP-signed manifest; not Apple-notarized; independently maintained; not official Alby.

Source/download: [https://github.com/hudhaifahz/hub/releases/tag/grynvault-rebalance-v0.1.0-rc.7](https://github.com/hudhaifahz/hub/releases/tag/grynvault-rebalance-v0.1.0-rc.7)

items.title: Bitcoin Arena: decentralized game & prediction market platform live on testnet4
items.text:
Hi there,

We built Bitcoin Arena: games and prediction markets on Bitcoin. It is fully decentralized. There is no company running the rounds, no central server and no custodian. Anyone can run a node, and anyone can offer an app. It’s live on testnet4, and we need people outside the team to try both.

There’s no token and nothing to buy. Test sats are free and have no value.

Anyone can run a node

* Install it on Windows, macOS or Linux. A setup window walks you through it.
* Post a bond on Bitcoin and take a seat.
* Host apps, verify rounds and earn a share of the fees.
* No permission needed. Your bond is your ticket in.

Anyone can offer an app

* Write your game and sign it, and any node can host it.
* The nodes replay every round with your rules.
* There’s no approval and no listing fee.
* You earn 2% of every paid round in your app.

How a round stays honest

* A Bitcoin block hash draws the committee of nodes, so nobody picks who decides.
* Stakes lock in a Fedimint federation run by the nodes.
* A result counts only when 5 of 7 nodes confirm the same one, and anyone can object for 10 minutes.

How you can help

* Run a node on testnet4 and tell us where setup was hard.
* Build a small app and tell us what’s missing in the docs.
* Play Tick Tock Next Block, Rock Paper Scissors or the 15-minute Bitcoin Up or Down market and try to break it.

Would you run a node or build an app on this? If not, what’s stopping you? Honest criticism helps us most. Reply here or join us:

items.title: Loyalty/Rewards and Other Monetary Scams: The Points Guy (Net Interest)
items.text:
**Here's an interesting (but dated) one... from the amazing Substack "Net Interest."**

I had occasion today to look through point and reward economics, and next to central banking or sex trafficking or whatever it must be one of the most despicable industries out there. It's well-known that loyalty cards/rewards schemes are fiat money-printing scams that, at best, saddles the user with a below-mininum wage job (https://stacker.news/items/869415).

...but it's good for the companies running these schemes. (Yea, no shit: the money printing/issuing was always great, and under shitty monetary regime there's an incentive for everyone to become a bank or a bank-like entity #[743123](https://stacker.news/items/743123), https://stacker.news/items/1329539)

It's a typical example where businesses do things **against the interest of their customer** (thus, it's dishonest) *while looking* like they're providing you with extra benefits. Somebody should call Lizzy (Warren!). (Also, it's one area where the European Union, in its infinite overlording wisdom, made a limiting regulation that was *actually good* for us Europooreans! By capping interchange fees, they basically outlawed rewards programs and saved/spared 500 million Europeans the time/necessary effort to play these silly money games.)

***

In the age of card networks and (FX) spreads (https://stacker.news/items/1586158) and costs to merchants, the COST and BENEFITS of these (Ponzi?) schemes become entirely intransparent where everyone, like in democracy, think they might get one over on someone else.

At best, it's a selection-biased gamble where **sophisticated consumers take advantage by optimizing the terms/conditions/value of the whole scheme vs naive consumers** who mistakenly believe they can/will win, while the house (as every properly set-up gamble) wins. The naive consumers will inevitably make some sort of error in their financial behavior (overdrafts, not enough spending, not maximizing rewards, too small fish such that annual fee eats up all other benefits).

The most well-known examples here are

* **bank deposits**: people hold too much cash at low-yielding bank accounts vs what they could/optimally should keep in higher-yielding savings accounts. The difference, while maaaybe sometimes convenient for the customer, end up in aggregate securing a massive windfall (=cheap financing) for the banks
* **life insurance products**: life insurance is usually priced very affordably and attractively for the buyer, which the insurance company isn't doing out of ignorance or stupidity but because they know from experience that some portion of the buyers (accidents, life circumstances changing, or just neglect) will let their policies lapse after having paid for a few years, meaning free money for the company, or worse, sell it back to the company at a great discount (=again, free money)

Here's the conclusion from a Fed paper on the subject from a few years ago:

> regardless of income, sophisticated individuals profit from reward credit cards at the expense of naïve consumers. To probe the underlying mechanisms, we exploit bank-initiated account limit increases at the card level and show that reward cards induce more spending, leaving naïve consumers with higher unpaid balances \[...]
> Naïve consumers might underestimate these payments and incur costs from usage. Sophisticated consumers, in contrast, might rake in the benefits while avoiding the payments and thus profit from usage

Here's the graph they use to display the idea (sorted by FICO scores, but the same point stands)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162147)

*tl;dr*, the area between the curves is larger on the negative side than the positive side, thus a) redistributing from naive to sophisticated, but more importantly b) makes the entire scam profitable to the company to run: What it has to pay the sophisticated winners is less than what they manage to extract from the idiot losers.

## The entire edifice is a combination of beggar-thy-neighbor and race to the bottom, with misperception and money illusion becoming key features.

From our pal Matt Levine in a recent Money Stuff piece

> banks make a lot of their money from depositor inattention: When interest rates go up, bank customers mostly don’t move their money, because it would be a pain, so banks can pay below-market interest rates on their deposits.
> You could have similar worries about life insurance, or annuities, or mortgages: Lots of financial products are built (and priced) based on assumptions about customer inattention.

The strategy is that you intentionally misprice (underprice) your service, banking on the fact that, in aggregate, enough people who opt in for this juicy, nice-looking offers will make enough errors that the few sophisticated customers who take perfect, optimized advantage of the mispricing won't cost the company.

***

ANYWAY, **Marc Rubenstein walks through the logic and economics of loyalty programs** and points(!) to some of the intricate cross-subsidized and legal/economic oddities with these programs:

> A key question in the whole points dynamic is how much partners pay for miles. Avios Group deferred revenue at a rate of 0.88 pence per point on the stock it issued in 2023, its highest rate in many years. The consumer value of points varies widely according to how they are used, but The Points Guy puts the value of Avios at around 1.2 pence per point, so the benefit to the consumer is clear. 
> Because the airline can adjust the redemption rate to encourage the use of rewards in ways that reduce their marginal cost, it is able to offer rewards to card issuers at a discount.2 In this way, reward programs can generate profits for both issuers and airlines while generating loyalty to both, a significant positive sum outcome.

## “By minting points, airline companies are able to lock in substantial cash flows.”

> Online points-monitoring sites posting point “valuation” tables on a regular basis because of course the offers change and of course the issuer of this fake, unusable money manipulate it to their advantage.
> The only problem is that competition has been driving up the rate at which card companies pay rewards. Over the last 12 months, American Express has paid out 1.07% of purchase volume in rewards, up from 0.80% ten years ago. Other card issuers have seen similar reward inflation. Capital One paid out 1.29% of purchase volume in 2022, up from 0.80% in 2013. And Discover paid out 1.43%, up from 0.94%. 
> American Express was initially exempt from the EU rules, so my British Airways co-branded card remained unaffected. In 2018, though, the courts brought Amex into line. Fortunately, American Express agreed to eat the cost. My BA Premium Plus card continues to pay 1.5 Avios points for every £1 spent, equivalent to around 1.8% on the basis of The Points Guy’s 1.2 pence per Avios valuation. I guess I do pay £250 per year for the privilege, and Amex likely bought the points at a steep discount (in particular the batch they acquired in 2020 to help the airline out of a liquidity squeeze).

JUST that gives us a few intransparent economic flows:

* First: The Amex bailout of BA during ‘rona, purchasing made-up points at cheap discount… even if Amex nominally loses \~1.3% per dollar of EU transactions, if what they hand over to the customer in rewards (=made-up BA money) was acquired at well below par, there’s still a profit in it for the card company.
* Second, to recoup the yearly card fee of 250 quid, a user needs to transact just below £14,000 a year, basically most of the discretionary card spending for a normal (Europoorean) person… and that’s not giving you pounds back, but made-up BA money you must do some additional trixing (in their webshops, for air fares, for lounge access or extra luggage etc) to benefit from.

## “there are clear subsidies at play. Someone, somewhere is subsidizing my points habit – no longer the merchant, it is now other BA or Amex customers. Indeed, such subsidies are the most controversial aspect to the model.”

I don't quite understand what this percentage is referring to (a larger share of Amex revenues are going back to users than before...?) but it seems to suggest that there is some sort of competitive pressure to close this rent-seeking gap

items.title: Review of David Berri's Sports Economics, Chapter 1
items.text:
I started reading David Berri's textbook on Sports Economics in preparation for my upcoming [course](https://stacker.news/items/1586317), which has been approved by one committee and only needs approval by another before it gets the go-ahead.  I figured it would be helpful to both myself, and fun for stackers, to review each chapter as I go along.

## Chapter 1: It's Just Supply and Demand

Chapter 1 covers basic supply and demand theory that you would encounter in any introductory econ course, but he motivates it using sports examples, such as ticket prices, trading card prices, and player salaries.

I especially liked how he walked us through an analysis of a statement made by Obama, to show us why it's wrong.  Here's Obama's statement:

> "The biggest change I'd \[make right now as commissioner] is to figure out how to price tickets so that ordinary people can go to the games.  I mean, I think that ticket prices have gotten so high, and I understand that if salaries are high, ticket prices are going to be high, but you know, you hate to think that the only person that can go to a game is somebody who's got a corporate account."

Berri uses supply and demand to walk us through why, given that the supply of NBA tickets is pretty stable year-to-year because of a fixed schedule and fixed stadium capacities, the only explanation for rising ticket prices is growing demand.  Thus, rising ticket prices can't be caused by high player salaries; instead, it's more likely that both ticket prices and player salaries are high because of growing demand for the sport.

Along the way, he covers some other topics that are common to introductory econ courses:

* The effect of price controls, using salary caps as an example
* The difference between positive and normative statements, using "why do they get paid so much to bounce a ball" as an example
* The difference between deductive and inductive reasoning (no example given, but he said the rest of the book will be framed around that organization;  I think another way to say that is theory and empirics)

## What is this, a book for jocks?

The only thing I didn't like about the chapter was the problems at the end of the chapter.  I was expecting some problems that ask the student to use supply and demand creatively, like forecasting the price change in response to a new stadium buildout, for example.  Instead, the problems at the end are basically questions whose answers are given directly in the text of the chapter.  In other words, they felt like memorization questions.  And they were super simple too.  I'll be honest, I couldn't help but think that this book was written for dummies.  *Maybe it was written for jocks??*

In any case, I think smarter questions would have behooved the book well.  Maybe they're just simple because it's the introductory chapter.  We'll see if the problems get smarter as we go along.

## A problem for the stackers

But anyway, since the problems were too simple, I decided to make one up myself.  Let's see if stackers can handle some basic intro econ questions, as applied to the sports industry:

1. The MLB is considering the imposition of a salary cap.  Use supply and demand to illustrate how player salaries are determined currently, without a salary cap, then use the same diagram to illustrate what might happen to player salaries after the salary cap.  Use the diagram to discuss how player salaries might be affected immediately depending on the level of the new salary cap.  Explain how the salary cap might change players' decision-making during free agency (how will they choose which team to play for if all teams can only offer them the same salary?)

items.text:
@spiral published The Long Road to Bitcoin Payments https://stacker.news/items/1603307/r/Scoresby last week and got quite a good discussion going here and on [Github](https://github.com/spiralxyz/bitcoin-payments/discussions/1).

Today, they are out with a summary of the community's response.

> **1. Global entrepreneurs, human or agent, earning in bitcoin.**
> **2. Agentic payments.**
> **3. Self-custody as stablecoins get more regulated and freezable.**

The guys on PBJ also did a recap of the discussion on their most recent episode, which is an interesting listen:

https://x.com/PresidioPod/status/2118070779959017814

There were two things that caught my attention in this conversation. First, @moneyball makes the point that it is surprising that the gray-market areas haven't seemed to find much use for bitcoin. 

# Why haven't the porn sites, online gambling dens, and illegal markets shown much interest in bitcoin payments?

While moneyball doesn't mention it, he made me think of Starbackr https://stacker.news/items/135689 https://stacker.news/items/67590 and after a little poking around it looks like they had some trouble with the App Store allowing zaps https://stacker.news/items/219407 but eventually managed a workaround https://stacker.news/items/224893 but then pivoted to AI https://stacker.news/items/250739 and quietly shut down -- at least the main starbackr website is no longer reachable (wayback machine last crawled it in [July 2024](https://web.archive.org/web/20240727123411/https://starbackr.com/) and shows a redirect to getcurrent.io -- last crawled by the wayback machine in Dec 2024 -- although you can still reach the [starbackr docs page](https://docs.starbackr.com/)). These guys seem to have made as good a run as any at delivering a bitcoin powered OnlyFans. What happened?

It seems that the same is true for online gambling (although maybe this story about [Iranian gambling sites](https://www.reuters.com/investigations/illicit-iranian-gambling-network-helped-pull-off-4-billion-sanctions-dodge-2026-07-31/) is a hint that bitcoin is being used in this manner? possibly we are all just too goody-goody to get invited to the illegal tables?).

I don't believe that traceability is the answer. As far as I can tell, porn sites and online gambling are mostly using credit card payments and tradfi banking, which is even worse for privacy. 

Spiral says that a lot of responses pointed out that there isn't any demand for bitcoin. But that seems to be answering the question with the question itself -- why isn't there any demand? 

# Surely someone needs money that no one can stop you from sending or receiving?

items.title: When “Nothing Ever Happens” Become the Pennies-Before-Steamroller Trade
items.text:
I’ve never thought I have much of a trading acumen — not in the stock market, not in timing the Bitcoin market (which I clearly cannot…), not in prediction markets. Prediction markets is the [biggest thing I’ve (mostly) changed my mind](https://stacker.news/items/1556891) on this year, and Predyx has been the outlet for me to play in this degenerate pool of trading nonsense. (Maybe I'll move on to the big leagues one day if I feel confident enough!)

And because most things on prediction markets are nonsense, they’re *ripe* for an age-old trading strategy called **Nothing Ever Happens**; it’s basically to buy No contracts on more or less everything. Matt Levine [summarizing](https://archive.md/B2XkB) the idea:

>  the “Nothing Ever Happens” factor: Bettors on prediction markets seem to be biased in favor of stuff happening (because that’s more fun), so betting “No” on every event seems to have positive returns. \[…] because betting heavy favorites is boring and betting underdogs is exciting, there might be positive returns to taking the other side and betting on the heavy favorites.

If there’s a contract like **Will X happen in 2026?** Den is likely a holder on the No side.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163325)

Yes, fine: I have some directional bets too (like the F1 or the Brazilian election… and look how those turned out).

In Prospect Theory, a branch of behavioral economics, there’s the phenomenon of a “sure thing” — basically that people are willing to unreasonably pay up to shove a risk/payoff from 1% (99%) to 0% (100%). *All insurance markets are predicated on this insight* (and customer inattention/monetary misperception…https://stacker.news/items/1598937, https://stacker.news/items/1598123)

At Predyx, I’ve found myself harvesting this quite a bit. I routinely pump sats into [the Saylor trade](https://beta.predyx.com/market/will-strategy-reach-905000-btc-holdings-from-purchases-completed-in-2026-1776280186) … (https://stacker.news/items/1602523) "Will Duolingo add bitcoin payments?" "Will Cuba be attacked by the US?" Those sorts of ridiculous contracts.  

All three technically carry some risk but are *basically* just interest rate trades at this point, and I’m happy to harvest that (steamroller) return.

Same goes for the “Will Bitcoin Hit $x? this year?” which *do* have some hedging benefits but largely suffer from exactly that same excitement mispricing.

## 2 Other Lessons from Trading

1. Which I learned in the Argentina game against Egypt (?) when they were down like crazy but managed to turn it around. While on a walk I saw Argentina trading at 1% and I YOLOd in the biggest Predyx order I’ve ever made — I keep sizes *very* conservative; the emphasis is on *play* in “play money” — and made a total *killing* on this contract. Consequently, in the F1 trade I bought Verstappen contracts at roughly 0. Didn’t care that I’m throwing away sats as long as there was still a mathematical possibility that this flying Dutchman could turn things around — a feat we’ve seen him accomplish in the recent past. (This was also a nice hedge to my 30,000 sats on Antonelli winning, which is but two points of guaranteed now.)
2. When you’re playing the safety/arbitrage/steamroller trades, getting even a single trade wrong is *extremely expensive*… If I’m capturing tons of different 95-5 trades, and all bets are equal-sized (which they are not, and I can monitor/trade on event news etc), getting *one* trade wrong obliterates the profits of nineteen others. *Ouch*. When I do things like this I better not be wrong… More specifically, I size the positions accordingly. A few months ago I wasn’t particularly convinced that the **Saylor>905k BTC contract would be a No**, so all I did was trade around and place small bets (100s of sats). After monitoring their recent Monday-reported purchases and realizing how far away they were from 905k + mapping out the BTC/USD and STRC scenarios, I grew more convinced that this will not work out for Mr. Saylor and his choirbois (*this* side of 2026 — or ever…?)

This win rate (83%) is *way too low* for largely speaking doing steamroller/Nothing-Ever-Happens trades. (Then again, I *have* taken some directional and spicy bets, e.g., during the World Cup, so maybe that’s why)

**In the Brazil election bet yesterday**, I noticed how uncomfortable I was with such a directional bet — on the bloody finish line. The Polymarket reference rate wobbled a little bit, and Den instantly took some profits. *If you hold a contract at ^0.71, there’s a long way down to 0 if you’re wrong.*

…and, election tampering or as fate would have it, I got to experience exactly that. What’s worse, I had timed my social engagements such that I wasn’t in a position to trade *during the most critical hours*. Stupid.

That was an unforeseen/unexpected error. It’s not just *trading* the contracts on their own merits but *whether* I can, practically speaking, make them work. That’s a good lesson, too.

items.title: Financialization Everywhere: Starbucks and SN style (TDE, Jeff Degner)
items.text:
We've talked about this a lot: https://stacker.news/items/1598123, https://stacker.news/items/743123 https://stacker.news/items/869415

## Under a broken monetary system, EVERY COMPANY becomes money-printing banks

Airlines? *Banks*.
Card companies? *Banks*.
Universities? *Banks*
Hotels? *Baaaaanks*
Fintech firm Revolut? TOTALLY a *bank*.

...the latter is literally a bank, which issues fiat-denominated loans etc (https://stacker.news/items/1578425) but *also* prints points that conveniently plug into *other* shitcoin companies (airlines, hotels etc). 

**The ultra-financialization of everything...**

> In January 2002, shortly after the launch of the Starbucks Card, Michael Casey was its CFO and he reportedly gave a novel description of how Starbucks would use those funds. According to Allen Eslekin, the original Starbucks Card [program manager](https://peakportfolio.com/starbuckscard/), Casey was elated: **the program represented “a $20 million interest free loan from our customers”** that would reduce their reliance on banks for loans and operating cash.

Yeah, that's not how the customers think of them... but that's *entirely* what they are.

> In 2019, AIER contributor [J.P. Koning](https://aier.org/people/j-p-koning/) reiterated this illustration in his [*Moneyness*](https://www.moneyness.ca/2019/08/starbucks-monetary-superpower.html) blog. There, he explained that balances on gift cards amounted to $1.6 billion and “simultaneously function as a loan to Starbucks,” and customers are “providing the company with free debt.”

Love that. While JP's stance on Bitcoin has been between disappointing and retarded, he is/was spot on for this. One of the few online articles that have, in one fell swoop, altered my perspective.

![](https://m.stacker.news/165540)

## Are Cowboy Credits Shitcoins?

I mean, of course they are. 

SAME THING. They're interest-free finances for k00b et al. You can *call them* prepaid balances all you want, but if capital has a cost (Lightning channels, operational costs etc), then anything SN doesn't need to keep/hold one-for-one are freebies. *Duh*. (Fine, they're bitcoin-denominated liabilites, so that's less great if/when bitcoin appreciates, but if it doesn't?!)

...That they decay "fast" or can always be turned into SN-relevant services (posts, zaps, comments) is immaterial. Same goes for Starbucks:

> Lenders of money expect dollars back. Not so with a Starbucks gift card. The terms for a gift card purchase make it clear that the balance is “nonrefundable” and that it “may not be redeemed for cash,” unless required by law. What is owed is coffee or other Starbucks merchandise of the holder’s choice at an uncertain location sometime in the future.

## "According to their Q3 2026 SEC filing, Starbucks holds over $1.8 billion in “stored value card liability and current portion of deferred revenue.”"

> The economy of gift cards must also grapple with another reality: lost and forgotten cards. “Breakage” is the accounting term for those cards that are lost in the back of your kitchen junk drawer or that slid between your bucket seats.

My friend running partnerships for a certain old-school/fiat shitcoin (=loyalty) program confirms this... Breakage is *sort of* the point. The BEST possible money for them. \_I wonder what the "Breakage" equivalent is for Stacker and CC. If k00b et al were to produce income statements and balance sheet for their business (which, presumably, they do to investors/annual report style), **where would outstanding and non-used CCs sit?!**

> What breakage can’t do is produce cash. What it can do is to goose the earnings reports that shareholders and banks use to assess investment and lending decisions. In [FY 2025](https://investor.starbucks.com/news/financial-releases/news-details/2025/Starbucks-Reports-Q4-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2025-Results/default.aspx), Starbucks’ operating cash flow fell by 22 percent compared to the [previous year](https://investor.starbucks.com/news/financial-releases/news-details/2025/Starbucks-Reports-Q4-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2025-Results/default.aspx).

This isn't quite true. The cash was *given to Starbucks up front*! So the booking of breakage doesn't produce cash, sure, the company *had the cash all along*. That's what an interest-free loan MEANS.

> In this inflationary environment, holding a Starbucks gift card subjects one to an inflation tax. Prepaid cards experience a loss of purchasing power in the same way that holding cash balances do. Two years ago, that $25 gift card may have purchased five drinks at $5, but now may only get you four at $6.25 each.

We have a similar situation going on with CCs and bitcoin, since bitcoin's exchange rate travels/trades structurally *downward*. A CC created (and unused, unredeemed) at almost any point in the last two years is worth *less than it was when it was created*. Consumer missing out.

items.title: Microsoft is a Financial Engineer: Cash Flow Questions (FT, Kim & Armstrong)
items.text:
**Back to stock analysis basics!** [https://stacker.news/items/85150\&#x36](https://stacker.news/items/85150&#x36);**,** https://stacker.news/items/836811

*How's Microsoft doing?!*

![](https://m.stacker.news/164439)

## IT's All Just Financial Engineering?!

*Always has been*, idiot. https://stacker.news/items/1604239, https://stacker.news/items/1598123

> Last week, we wrote about how investors in the hyperscalers — Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle — are suddenly taking the decline in the companies’ free cash flow very seriously. (As, naturally, are the rating agencies — S\&P Global cut the outlook on Meta to negative just the other day, citing “significant uncertainty around capex and free operating cash flow”.)
> Microsoft stands out — it appears that, unlike its peers, it is not spending most or all of its cash profits that operations bring in. Correspondingly, Microsoft is the only one of the bunch with positive stock market returns over the last, bruising month:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164440)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164441)

and we care about this *why?*

> Investors like to look at free cash flow because metrics like operating profit and net income capture investment spending only through a smoothed measure (depreciation) and **do not capture swings in working capital items** (such as inventory, receivables and payables) that can dramatically affect a company’s economic position. Hyperscaler investors are, understandably, focused almost exclusively on the investment just at present.

* **GOOD** free cash flow is "fundamental profitability of the business." Selling stuff, you know, the good ole' fashioned reason to be in commerce. (LOL, say the diluting treasury companies... you can just scam your shareholders! https://stacker.news/items/1292636)
* **BAD** free cash flow is about financing (don't mention it to Saylor): terms, timing, BNPL on a corporate level, basically. 

> For example, a business might be able to pay its suppliers very slowly, while extracting instant payment from customers, which creates a growing stream of cash so long as sales are expanding.

## "This sort of financial engineering is not cheating and the company is admirably transparent about it."

> It is a source of real cash that can pay bills, be invested or simply collect interest. Indeed, there is a whole class of businesses that do nothing but co-ordinate various pools of capital with different financing arrangements. **They are called banks.** But free cash flow from financial engineering is often more volatile, less sustainable and harder to scale than cash that flows from profitable non-finance operations.

lol *sick buuuuurn!*

> Dave Zion of Zion Research Group [thinks](https://www.zionresearchgroup.com/blog/microsoft-s-free-cash-flow-would-be-negative-if-not-for-financial-engineering/) that *all* of Microsoft’s free cash flow comes from financial engineering. He thinks this engineering takes four main forms:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164442)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164443)

> The total of these and a few smaller adjustments is $75.3bn last year — more than 100 per cent of the company’s free cash flow. This does not mean that Microsoft is somehow hoodwinking investors. Powerful companies can extract good financial terms from suppliers, customers and investors and these terms have real value.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164444)

*Financial engineer? YES, I AM!* https://stacker.news/items/1514881?commentId=1514971

TL;DR, if you wanna fake (some portion) of your success, you can just print shares. In Saylor's case, it's to pay for expenses and interest to other shareholders (=Ponzi structure); for Microsoft it's to pay for employee compensation and capex.
